chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Prince Ivan, the Witch Baby, and the Little Sister of the Sun
chapters.artPrompt: a little prince on a black horse leaping through the open window of a rosy cloud castle hanging in the sky, below a giant baby-shaped witch chasing across the ground, stars twinkling, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago a little Prince Ivan was born who could not speak. His father and mother hardly looked at him, and he lived in the stables with the horses. The old groom knew everything. "A sister is born to you," he said, "a witch with iron teeth. She will grow like a seed of corn. Ask your father for his best horse, and ride to the end of the world." Ivan asked, and those were the first words he had ever spoken. He galloped away on a great black horse with silver trappings.

He asked everyone he met if this was the end of the world. Two old women were sewing their lives away. "When our needles are used up, we shall die," they said. A giant called Tree-rooter was tearing up the great oaks. A giant called Mountain-tosser was hurling mountains about. "When my work is done, I die," said each one. At last Ivan came to the end of the world. There hung a castle made of cloud, like red roses. The little sister of the Sun opened her window, and the black horse leapt in.

Apples of youth are magic apples from the old tales. Anyone who eats one becomes young again, however old and bent they may be. The two old women who sewed all their lives ate Ivan's apples, and their gray hair turned black as the raven.

Ivan played happily in the castle of cloud, but he grew sad. From the top turret he saw his father's palace far away, broken and roofless. "The witch has eaten them," he thought, and wept. The little sister of the Sun gave him a magic comb, a magic brush, and two apples of youth. "Go and see," she said, "though I would rather you stayed." He threw the brush on the plain, and mountains sprang up for Mountain-tosser. He threw the comb, and a forest sprang up for Tree-rooter. He gave the apples to the old women, who became young girls at once. They gave him a handkerchief that would turn into a lake.

In the ruined hall sat the witch baby, grown huge, sucking her thumb. "Eaten the father, eaten the mother," she muttered. "And now to eat the little brother." She shrank into a pretty little girl, and asked Ivan in. While she cooked supper he played a sad tune on the dulcimer. A little gray mouse crept out of a crack. Some say it was the wise old groom. "Run, Ivan! She is sharpening her iron teeth," it squeaked. Ivan fled, and the mouse jumped on the strings, so the music played on.
Prince Ivan on his black horse leaps through the castle window as the witch baby thunders along far below.

The witch baby tore the walls down and ran after him, towering over the trees. Ivan threw the handkerchief, and a deep lake made her swim. Tree-rooter piled oaks before her, and she gnawed through them with her iron teeth. Mountain-tosser flung mountains in her road, and she bit through those too. At the castle the little sister of the Sun flung the window wide. The black horse leapt in with Ivan safe. The witch baby demanded the great scales. She grew huge and jumped in, but Ivan's scale shot him up to the turret, safe and laughing. The witch gnashed her teeth till they broke. Ever since, Ivan and the Sun's sister play there, borrowing the stars for balls.

New word: turret — a small tower set on top of a castle wall. From the topmost turret of the cloud castle, Prince Ivan could see the whole wide world, far beyond the mountains and the forests, all the way to his father's palace.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Stolen Turnips and the Magic Tablecloth
chapters.artPrompt: a mossy wooden hut in a pine forest with dozens of tiny mischievous children dancing on the roof, each waving a white turnip, an old man looking up in astonishment, storybook illustration

blocks.text: An old man lived with a cross old woman who scolded all day. She wanted turnips, though the garden was full. "Sow them on top of the dovecot," she said. So the old man carried earth up the narrow stairs and sowed turnip seed. When the turnips grew fat, thieves stole the best of them every night. "Find the thieves," screamed the old woman, "and do not come back without them." Off went the old man into the forest, without his dinner.

Deep in the wood he found a hut full of chattering. On the stove lay a heap of blankets that laughed and stirred. Out tumbled dozens of little queer children, and every one held a turnip. "We stole the turnips," they cried. "We will pay for them." They gave him dinner from a magic tablecloth. "Tablecloth, turn inside out," they taught him to say, and it covered itself with every good dish. At "turn outside in" it cleaned itself spotless. The old man carried the tablecloth home, singing in his creaky voice.

New word: dovecot — a little house for pigeons, often set on the top of a roof or tower. The old woman made her husband carry earth up the narrow stairs, so that a turnip bed could grow on top of the family dovecot.

But at night the old woman hid the tablecloth in her iron chest. More turnips were stolen, and again he went to the children. This time they gave him a goat with a cold in its head. "Sneeze, goat," said the old man, and gold pieces flew from it all ways. The old woman grabbed the gold, then hid that goat in the bushes too. A third time turnips vanished, and a third time he trudged to the hut.

Now the children gave him a wooden whistle-pipe. He blew in it, and out jumped three lively whips that beat him till he blew them back inside. "Take it home," laughed the children. "That will put everything right." At home the old woman snatched the whistle. "Whatever you do, don't blow in it," said the old man. She blew, of course. The three whips beat her till she confessed everything. "The tablecloth is in the iron chest. The goat is in the bushes. I wanted all the gold myself." So the tablecloth and the goat came home, and there was peace at last.
Dozens of little queer children dance on the hut roof and wave their stolen turnips at the old man.

But next morning she scolded again, out of mere habit. She made the old man carry her up the narrow stairs in a flour sack, held in his strong teeth. "Are we at the top?" she kept screaming. "Very near," said the old man. As he opened his mouth, the sack slipped. Bump, bump, bumpety bump, all the way down. After that the hut was quiet. The old man lived alone with his magic goat, his tablecloth, and his whistle. Often he visited the little queer children, who were always dancing on the roof.

Kasha is a warm dish of grain, something like porridge, eaten in Russia at almost every meal. The little queer children gave the old man a plain bowl of kasha. It had no magic in it at all, but hunger made it taste fine.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Golden Fish
chapters.artPrompt: a golden fish rising from stormy green waves under a black sky, an old fisherman on the dark shore calling out with raised hands, white foam flying, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Beside the blue sea lived an old fisherman and his old wife, in a hut of earth and logs. One evening his net came in heavy, and in it glittered a golden fish. "Old man, do not kill me," said the fish with a human voice. "Throw me back, and some day I may be of use to you." The kind old man threw it back, and asked for nothing at all. "Ask anything you wish," said the fish, and sank in golden flashes.

But his wife scolded him. "Ask for bread," she said. Then a trough for the bread. Then a new hut. Each time the old man stood on the shore and called, "Head in air and tail in sea. Fish, fish, listen to me." Each time the fish said, "Go home." A loaf of white bread waited. Then a painted trough. Then a fine new hut, with a glittering brass samovar. Still the old woman was not content.

New word: samovar — a tall brass urn that boils water for tea. It stands in the middle of the table, and everyone fills a glass from it. In Russia no tea table is quite complete without its shining, bubbling samovar.

"I am tired of being a peasant," she cried. "I want to be a lady." The hut became a brick house with servants, and she made the old man her doorkeeper. Then she tired of being a lady. "I want to be Tzaritza," she said. A palace rose with a golden roof, with generals and soldiers crying hurrah. Then she wanted more still. "I will be ruler of the seas, and all the fishes shall be my servants."
The golden fish rises out of the stormy sea while the old man calls from the dark shore.

This time the fish came up out of a storm, and said nothing at all. It turned over and went down into the deep sea. The old man walked home slowly, afraid of what he would find. The palace was gone. The trumpets were silent. There stood the little old hut, and there sat his wife in a ragged dress, cleaning a saucepan and singing. This time she was glad to see him. They drank tea without sugar, and the old man fished happily ever after. He never caught the golden fish again.

A fish that speaks with a human voice is an old wish-granter of Russian tales. The kind old man asked for nothing at all. But every wish his wife asked from greed slipped away like water, until nothing was left but the little old hut.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Alenoushka and Her Brother
chapters.artPrompt: a small white lamb weeping on a river bank among tall reeds at sunset, sparkling water below with a gentle sad face reflected deep down, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Two orphan children set out to walk through the wide world. The girl was Alenoushka, and the boy was her little brother Vanoushka. One day the sun burned the plain, and their throats grew dry as sand. Vanoushka found the hoofmark of a horse, full of water. "Drink from a horse's hoofprint and you will turn into a foal," said his sister. Next a cow's hoofprint glittered. "A calf you would become," she said. But at a tiny sheep's footprint he could bear no more, and he drank. In a moment he was a little white lamb, frisking round his weeping sister.

A fine gentleman rode by the hayrick where Alenoushka sat weeping. The lamb frisked before her and licked the tears from her face. "Come and live in my house," he said, "you and your lamb." He married Alenoushka, and they lived so happily that good people rejoiced. The little lamb never grew any bigger, but followed her everywhere she went.

In the old tales, water lying in a hoofprint carries a spell. Drink from a horse's print and you may become a foal, or from a cow's print a calf. Clean water from a well was the only safe drink for a thirsty traveller.

One day a wicked old witch with one tooth came begging at the door. She put a spell in the wine, so that Alenoushka grew pale and thin. Then she offered a cure. "Bathe secretly in the river this afternoon," she said. At the river the witch sprang out. She tied a heavy stone round Alenoushka's neck and threw her into the deep water. Then the witch put on her white dress, and took her place in the house. Only the little lamb had seen it all.
The little white lamb stands weeping on the river bank while a sad voice answers from under the water.

The lamb went to the river every morning and every evening, and would not eat. The witch hated him, and ordered the cauldrons heated and the knives sharpened. At the bank the little lamb sang a farewell song to the water. And from the bottom of the river a sad voice answered. A servant heard the wonder, and told his master. They came with nets of fine silk, and drew Alenoushka out as if she were asleep. They untied the stone, and she woke more beautiful than ever. The lamb leapt to her, and became her brother again, laughing in the sunshine. The fine gentleman turned the witch out of the house, and she fled shrieking to the deep woods.

New word: hayrick — a big, rounded pile of hay standing in a field, like a soft giant's hat. Alenoushka sat down and wept in its shade, and it was there that the fine gentleman on the black horse first saw her.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and the Princess Vasilissa
chapters.artPrompt: a huge golden fire-bird with flaming wings eating grain in an open field at dawn, a black horse pinning one fiery wing to the earth, an archer watching from a great oak, storybook illustration

blocks.text: A young archer served a mighty Tzar, and rode a horse of power with eyes like fire. One day he rode through a silent forest where no bird sang. On the path lay a golden feather, glittering like a flame. "Leave it," said the horse of power. "If you take it, you will be sorry." But the archer took the feather to the Tzar. "A feather is not a fit gift," said the Tzar. "Bring me the bird itself, or your head shall fall."

The horse told him what to do. At midnight a hundred sacks of maize were scattered in an open field. At dawn the fire-bird came flying from the other side of the world, huge and flaming. It dropped to eat the maize. The horse wandered near, then stepped on one fiery wing and pressed it to the ground. The archer bound the bird with three ropes, and carried it to the palace.

The fire-bird is the brightest bird in all the Russian tales. Its feathers glow like flames in the dark, and one golden feather can light a whole room. That is why the Tzar would not be satisfied with a feather, but wanted the bird itself.

Now the Tzar wanted a bride. "Bring me the Princess Vasilissa from the land of Never, at the edge of the world." With a silver tent and rich wines, the archer rode to the shore of the blue sea. There the Princess rowed in a little silver boat with golden oars. She came to taste the strange sweetmeats, and fell into a deep sleep. The archer carried her gently to the Tzar. But when she woke, she turned her face away from the old Tzar.

"My wedding dress lies under a great stone in the middle of the sea," she said. On the shore the horse pinned a giant lobster by the tail. "Let me go, and I will serve you," cried the lobster. It called all the lobsters of the sea, and they brought the golden casket. Still the Princess would not marry the Tzar. "No," she said, "until the man who brought me has done penance in boiling water." So they heated a great cauldron for the young archer.
The flaming fire-bird spreads its wings over the maize field while the horse of power pins one fiery wing.

The horse whispered, "Fear not. When the time comes, leap in boldly yourself." The Princess waved her hand over the cauldron, and some say she held something in it. The archer leapt, sank twice, and rose up more beautiful than ever. "This is a miracle," cried the Tzar, thinking of his gray beard. He climbed in after the archer, and that was the end of the old Tzar. The young archer was made Tzar in his place, and married the Princess Vasilissa. And the horse of power lived out its days in a golden stable.

New word: bogatir — one of the strong heroes of old Russia. The bogatirs sleep underground with their mighty horses until Russia has need of them. A horse of power, with eyes like fire and hoofs of iron, was such a horse as the bogatirs rode.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Salt
chapters.artPrompt: a small wooden sailing ship with patchwork sails and heaped white salt mounds approaching a hillside town with golden towers above a quiet harbour, blue sea and sunshine, storybook illustration

blocks.text: A rich merchant had three sons. The two elder brothers sailed off in fine ships, laden with gold and silks. The youngest was called Ivan the Ninny, because he had only ever played. At last Ivan begged for a ship of his own. His father gave him a little old ship, a cargo of rags, and a crew of ancient sailormen. A great wind threw them on an unknown island. In the middle of the island stood a white mountain. It was not snow. It was clean white Russian salt.

They threw the rags overboard, and loaded the little ship with salt. In a far town on a hill, no one had ever heard of salt. "White dust," laughed the Tzar of that town. "You must be a ninny." But in the palace kitchen Ivan slipped a pinch of salt into every dish. "It is the best soup I ever tasted," said the Tzar. The Tzaritza said so too, and the Princess. Ivan sold the salt for bags of gold, silver, and precious stones.

Long ago, salt was rare in faraway lands. Without salt, meat and soup taste flat and dull. Ships carried it across the sea like treasure, and a whole mountain of it, like Ivan found, was worth more than gold, silver, and precious stones.

The Princess came to see the little Russian ship before it sailed. While the anchor was shown to her, the wind filled the patched sails, and the ship slipped out to sea. Ivan comforted her, and they agreed to be married. Soon they met the two elder brothers' ships. When the brothers saw the Princess and the heaps of jewels, they ground their teeth. In the twilight they threw Ivan overboard into the dark blue sea.

But Ivan swam till sunrise, and then floated on a timber log. The current carried him to an island where a giant lived in a house as big as a mountain. "To-morrow your brother marries your Princess," said the giant. "Climb on my shoulders, and I will carry you there." He strode through the sea, splashing water from his ankles. Ivan ran into the wedding feast, and the Princess cried out with joy. "There is my true love, and not this man beside me," she said. The father turned the brothers out of doors, gave their ships to Ivan, and married him to the Princess.
The little ship, heaped with white salt and sailing on patched sails, comes to the hill town with golden towers.

At the feast the guests boasted, and Ivan could not hold his tongue. "I am the only man who rode on a giant's shoulders," he cried. At once the giant came striding up, roaring. "You promised not to boast of me, little man," he thundered. "It was the drink that boasted, not I," said Ivan. So Ivan gave the giant a barrel of wine, then a barrel of beer, then a barrel of mead. The giant drank them like little glasses, fell flat, and slept for three days. When he woke and saw the broken houses, he laughed. "After that, you may boast of me for a thousand years," he said, and went striding off into the sea.

New word: verst — an old Russian measure of distance, a little longer than a kilometre. When the giant strode through the sea, he left Ivan's blown-off hat five hundred versts behind him before he even thought of turning back for it.
